item.title: Windows has been slowing down every USB drive you plug in for 8 years, and one setting fixes it
item.itunes:title: Windows has been slowing down every USB drive you plug in for 8 years, and one setting fixes it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most of us use our USB devices the same way. We plug it in, drag some files across, wait for the copying to finish, and pull it out without a second thought. What most users never notice is that Windows quietly made a change to how it works back in 2018, and this change has been the default on Windows machines ever since. The idea was to make it safer to pull out a USB drive without needing to eject it and reduce the likelihood of losing any data in the process.

There's a trade-off to this, though, and there's no way to know exactly what unless you go looking for that information. Windows gives up some write performance to make that possible, because it no longer uses write caching for removable drives by default, which leads to slightly lower transfer speeds. How much that matters depends on the type of drive you're using, and what you're copying. Curious to know the difference, I grabbed a cheap USB 2.0 drive that lay on my desk and put it through an experiment I designed.

Windows changed how it treats your USB drives many years ago

And it didn't make much noise about it

The setting that I'm talking about is known as Quick Removal, and Microsoft switched it on by default with Windows 10 version 1809 in October 2018. Prior to that, the default option for all connected USB devices was called "Better performance." Unless you've gone looking for the setting and changed it yourself, that's how every USB drive, external SSD, and Thunderbolt drive you've plugged in since has been handled.

On the Microsoft Learn forums, what the two options do is fairly detailed. Quick Removal keeps the drive ready to be unplugged at any time, but at the same time WIndows can't cache writes to it.

On the other hand, Better Performance allows for write caching, which can make transfers faster, but you have to safely eject the drive before pulling it out. As you can imagine, this is just Windows choosing convenience and data safety over a bit of extra performance, which is a sensible trade-off considering how most users just pull out their removable drives without a second thought. The setting still exits in Windows 11, and it's hidden away under the Policies tab in your drive's properties.

5 ways to make your files transfer faster on Windows 11

Whether your PC is old or brand new, these tips will help speed up file transfers

1
By  Brian Burgess

I put both settings on the clock with a cheap USB 2.0 stick

With the same 6,000 tiny files and the same port, I measured the difference

To see how much Quick Removal costs in terms of time, I made a folder containing 6,000 small files, ranging from 4KB to 256KB each, for about 760MB in total. Small files are where write caching should have the biggest impact (theoretically speaking), since there's a lot of little bits of overhead for the cache to smooth over. I copied the folder to a cheap USB 2.0 stick, timed it, and then ran the same test with Better Performance enabled.

On Quick Removal, which is the default setting on Windows, the copy took about 11 minutes and 31 seconds to complete. Switching to Better Performance brought that down to 10 minutes and 31 seconds, which accounts for a full minute saved by changing the setting on a USB 2.0 stick that was never going to be particularly fast in the first place.

Do you really need to “safely” eject a USB drive?

The answer might surprise you

13
By  Patrick Hearn

How to change the default setting, and whether you should

It takes a single checkbox, but requires changing a habit you've built for years

Getting to the setting is rather straightforward, and you can flip it in thirty seconds on your desktop. Before that, though, there's an important question worth asking yourself, and it's whether the extra performance is worth changing the way you've been using your USB drives for years.

To get to the toggle, you'd have to right-click Start, open Device Manager, expand Disk drives, and look for your USB stick, or sticks, if there are multiple. Open its Properties, head over to the Policies tab, and here is where you'll find the Quick Removal policy at the top. If you've never changed it, that'll be the default. You can switch it from Quick Removal to Better Performance, and then you're done. Microsoft also recommends selecting "Enable write caching" on the device whenever Better Performance is toggled.

I've also observed that the setting doesn't immediately take effect, so it's worth going through a reboot cycle after you've toggled it. After the setting is changed, Microsoft also says that the policy that's set remains in effect if you disconnect it and then re-connect it to the same port, so you don't have to change the setting over and over again on each restart.

Should you change the policy to save some more time?

The question that remains is who should flip this setting, and my recommendation is that not everyone should do it, especially because it's built as a safeguard that's tailored to how people use their USB devices all the time.

It's a setting that's better fit for anyone who already waits for the eject prompt out of habit, who copies big folders of small files to the same drive often, and who'd rather have the minute back than the mental shortcut of pulling the stick the moment the window closes. It's also worth noting that the difference that I observed reflects the result of a single test, so the time savings may be more or less depending on the drive used and the type of file that's being copied.

item.title: One VLAN setting locked down my smart home and stopped every device from phoning home
item.itunes:title: One VLAN setting locked down my smart home and stopped every device from phoning home
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
With a modern smart home it feels like every cheap smart bulb, Wi-Fi camera, robot vacuum, and thermostat you buy requires an app account, connects to your local Wi-Fi, and immediately starts whispering telemetry data back to distant cloud servers.On a standard consumer router every device sits on a single flat local network. Your high-end workstation, your personal NAS containing family photos, and a $10 untrusted Chinese smart plug all share the exact same subnet with zero internal isolation.

Luckily there's a fix. I decided to configure a dedicated virtual local area network (VLAN) and a few strict firewall rules to sever unauthorized internet access for my IoT gear while keeping local communications intact. Smart home convenience shouldn't require surrendering your digital privacy. By implementing a dedicated IoT VLAN and blocking unwanted egress at your firewall, you can stop untrusted devices from snooping while keeping your home automation stack running locally.

6 things you need to know before setting up VLANs on your home network

VLANs are super handy for organizing your network, but you need to do some prep work first

3
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Why are IoT devices so chatty?

They rely on phoning home

IoT devices absolutely love to phone home. Smart devices are inherently chatty and that means they pose security risks because of their cloud-dependent business model. Most consumer smart devices are engineered to route commands through third-party servers (whether that's to your AWS or to your back-end apps) rather than operating locally. So many IoT devices constantly beacon out to foreign telemetry endpoints.

Each time an IoT device sends a ping out to a third-party cloud server, this puts your home at risk. It can be that hackers intercept the data being sent and therefore have access to information about your home or sometimes hackers can actually access your home network through your smart devices.

If a budget smart plug or IP camera running outdated firmware becomes compromised, a flat local network allows threat actors to pivot internally. This means that they can scan your NAS, desktop PCs, and sensitive shares with ease. Anything that's on the same flat local network is vulnerable.

How you can set up a VLAN to solve the issue

Ensure you adjust your firewall rules too

The solution to the problem for me was to set up a VLAN and tweak my firewall settings. This allowed me to segregate and restrict a lot of my IoT devices and create an airtight boundary for my smart devices.

An isolated IoT VLAN felt absolutely fundamental to me. In order to set it all up I first logged into my router settings and then created the IoT VLAN, assigning a dedicated 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network. Setting up a dedicated VLAN tag on your router or managed switch, paired with a dedicated SSID broadcasting strictly on the 2.4 GHz band, was the solution for me.

Once I had this all set up I migrated over all of my smart devices. I moved countless Wi-Fi bulbs, plugs, and cameras over to the new IoT SSID. It really made me realize just how many smart home devices I actually have on my network. I then assigned static DHCP leases for easier management.

Then I decided to adjust my firewall rules. I created rules allowing established/related traffic from my main network to IoT, allowing IoT to talk strictly to my Home Assistant server IP, and dropping all other outbound WAN traffic from the IoT subnet.

Writing these stateful firewall rules allows the IoT VLAN to talk to your local home assistant server so that local automations still function smoothly, but strictly blocks all WAN access (essentially internet access) and prevents the IoT network from initiating traffic back into your trusted primary network. If any of your smart devices are limited in functionality when they're not connected to the internet, this obviously won't work for them.

Some of your devices might not work without the cloud

But really, that's just a sign they should be replaced

You can see how much of a difference this makes by auditing your firewall logs. You'll see so many blocked connection attempts your smart devices make daily, confirming that your privacy lockdown is working. Depending on what devices you have as part of your smart home, some of them will react differently when you cut that cloud cord.

A lot of rebellious devices will create a dilemma. Some of those cheaper devices will brick or refuse to function if they can't ping an external NTP server or check in with their cloud mothership. Rather than allowing these devices onto your main flat local network, you're better off identifying which ones need local-only alternatives. Sometimes you can flash them with local firmware flashes like ESPHome/Tasmota but this isn't always the case.

Ensuring that your local smart home hub bridges the VLAN divide cleanly will allow local API control without exposing your broader network infrastructure. This will allow you to completely preserve your Home Assistant integration and any other automations that you have.

This single change can make a major difference to your security

You shouldn't have to worry every time your devices phone home

Building a smart home doesn't mean giving up your right to privacy. Implementing a single VLAN setting and blocking outbound traffic transforms your network from an open sieve into a secure private fortress. Stop letting budget smart gadgets phone home behind your back. Set up an isolated IoT VLAN today. Lock down your firewall and keep your smart home smart and private.

item.title: After a month with VS Code, Cursor, and Zed, I finally found the editor that gets out of the way
item.itunes:title: After a month with VS Code, Cursor, and Zed, I finally found the editor that gets out of the way
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I have spent years using VS Code, so switching between three different editors for a month was not something I expected to do. But I wanted to see whether newer options like Zed and Cursor could actually change the way I work. Instead of judging them after a quick test, I used each one for real coding tasks and paid attention to the small things that affect my day-to-day workflow. Some differences were obvious, while others only became clear after switching back and forth. By the end of the month, one editor stood out enough that I stopped thinking about switching again.

VS Code still does almost everything right

The editor that does almost everything

VS Code is still the editor I can open and start using without thinking. I have spent years with it, so the layout, shortcuts, file explorer, terminal, and Git tools all feel natural to me. Even after trying other editors for a month, I still find myself falling back on the same familiar workflow.

The biggest advantage is its enormous library of extensions. There is an extension for almost everything I might need, whether it is related to a language, framework, file format, debugging, productivity, or a small quality-of-life feature. That ecosystem makes VS Code incredibly flexible, especially when I want to customize the editor around a specific project.

But that flexibility comes with a cost. VS Code can feel heavy, particularly compared with newer, more lightweight editors. When I have a larger project open with several extensions running, I notice that it takes longer to start and can feel less responsive than I want. It is not painfully slow, but after spending time with faster editors, the difference becomes much easier to notice.

item.title: Every cheap QLC SSD is secretly two drives, and the fast one gets smaller the more you fill it
item.itunes:title: Every cheap QLC SSD is secretly two drives, and the fast one gets smaller the more you fill it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
When you're in the market for an NVMe SSD, you might encounter varying prices, and sometimes, getting the cheapest drive sounds like a good deal. After all, you're getting flash storage for your PC at the end of the day anyway, right?

Well, not quite. There are a couple of reasons why it's always worth a second look into what you might be potentially losing out on by going for the cheapest drive on the shelf. Not every storage device is created the same way, and that's true for M.2 NVMe SSDs as well. Depending on the type of NAND flash inside, two drives with the same capacity and sequential speeds may behave very differently once you fill them.

By going for the cheapest drives, which usually use QLC flash, you may be signing up for two drives in one, and the faster of which shrinks over time. Once it runs out, your experience can be quite sluggish, and the only fix would be to get another drive. Here's what you want to know before you buy.

Your QLC drive runs a second, faster drive on the same chips

It writes everything there first, sorts it out later, and it can exhaust pretty quickly

When it comes to flash memory, QLC stands for Quad-Level Cell, which means each cell stores four bits of data. This is the densest NAND you can buy in the consumer market. The reason why density is relevant at all is that more bits per cell means fewer cells for the same capacity, and that means a lower price per terabyte. That's why QLC-based SSDs are amongst the cheapest in the market.

The catch is that writing to a QLC cell is slow, and that is because the controller has to resolve one of sixteen voltage states to land four bits accurately, which is a process that takes time. What the drive effectively does to work around this is that it takes a slice of the same QLC cells and runs them in single-bit mode, storing just one bit each instead of four. In that mode, they can write faster and achieve a speed close to the speeds printed on the box.

What you'll never see on the box, though, is how far the drive falls once the fast region runs out. In TechPowerUp's test of the HPFX700, a $100 PCIe Gen 4 QLC drive, the difference was clear enough to change purchase decisions. The drive held close to 5GB/s at start, but behaved very differently when it started to fill up. The speed was sustained until 54GB was written, following which it dropped to 3.5GB/s. After 460GB out of 2TB had been written onto the drive, the performance collapsed to 130MB/s, a figure which the reviewers compared with a mechanical hard drive.

4 differences between QLC, TLC, and MLC SSDs

If you've heard of QLC, TLC, and MLC SSDs, these are the biggest differences between them.

By  Adam Conway

The fast drive is hiding inside your QLC NAND

And every file you write eats into that cache

Credit: Crucial

This means that everything you copy lands in this "fast" region first, and the drive folds it down into dense four-bit QLC later when it's idle. Take the Intel 660p for example, which was the first QLC-based PCIe SSD. Intel's product brief describes a dynamic architecture that changes how the drive's cells are configured to balance capacity against performance, although it stops short of spelling the cost.

A single cell running in fast single-bit mode holds a quarter of what it does packed with four bits, so the fast region always borrows four times its size in capacity from the rest of the drive. So, in theory, a full terabyte of QLC could yield about 256GB of fast single-bit storage, though real drives typically reserve a smaller dynamic cache that shrinks as the drive fills.

The fast drive isn't a separate chip that's bolted beside the slow one, but rather, it's carved out of the same QLC NAND, using whatever cells you haven't filled yet. So, the fast region and your storage are drawing from the same pool, but every file you keep is a block that can no longer run in fast mode.

Tom's Hardware observed exactly this in their testing of the 660p, noting that the fast region grows as you delete files and shrinks as you add them. On the 1TB model, that meant a generous 140GB of fast storage, but it fell to just 12GB once it was nearly full.

Here's why your NVMe SSD feels worse than a SATA SSD

Some NVMe SSDs can perform slower than quality SATA SSDs in certain workloads

By  Tanveer Singh

Don't swear off QLC drives yet, though

They're great for many workloads, but probably not the ones you have in mind

Now, I realize that everything I've said so far makes QLC sound like something you should avoid at all costs, and if you particularly dread your SSD's speeds falling down to hard-drive speeds, that's a reasonable concern and a valid reason to buy better. It is, however, an incomplete picture, and therefore worth understanding where it might actually make sense to spend less.

The first thing to keep in mind is that the performance drop-off only becomes a concern when you write more data in one go than the fast region could hold, for example, when a single continuous write exceeds the available pseudo-SLC cache. For most of what a PC does day to day, you never get close to that.

It's also worth keeping in mind that QLC SSDs are built for read-heavy, capacity-first storage where writes are infrequent and latency isn't the priority. A QLC drive is a fine home for a Steam library you install once and load for months, your media collection, or a bulk archive you barely touch. In all of those use-cases, the reads stay fast, and the capacity is cheap.

Always read about the SSD you're about to buy

Despite what it might seem like, QLC isn't automatically a bad buy, and given the current storage economy, you shouldn't be disqualifying yourself out of a bargain if you get a chance. If your SSD mostly stores games, media, or other data that you rarely rewrite, the cheaper drive makes the perfect sense, but if you're constantly moving large files, editing video, or filling the drive to the brim more frequently, TLC is where you'd get the best value.

item.title: I saved 300GB compressing my games, but going all-in was a mistake
item.itunes:title: I saved 300GB compressing my games, but going all-in was a mistake
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've been using Game Compressor recently to free up some storage space on my only 2TB NVMe drive. With many AAA titles taking over 100GB these days, a 2TB SSD can feel limiting quickly. Of course, I could uninstall the games I don't need every day and download them again when I want to play, but I'd rather avoid a 100GB download if I can. That's what convinced me to pay $6 instead of splurging on overpriced SSDs these days.

God of War alone gave me around 25GB back with LZX compression, and some other games came close, but the best part? I didn't see any difference in performance or loading times afterward. That said, I was careful with what games I chose to compress because not every game is worth compressing. In fact, even Game Compressor warns you against compressing games that use DirectStorage. And then there are games that don't even free up 1GB of space, making them hardly worth the time it takes to compress them.

DirectStorage games are where I draw the line

Because the potential performance hit is just not worth it

I like LZX compression so much because it not only frees up a lot of space, but the performance overhead has also been practically invisible in the games I've compressed, like God of War and Baldur's Gate 3. Windows decompresses those files on the fly using your CPU as the game accesses them, so you can play the game as if you never compressed it.

But with games that use DirectStorage, this file-system-level compression can work against it by preventing affected reads from using its optimized I/O path. Remember, DirectStorage has its own decompression pipeline, so LZX adds another layer of compression that doesn't help.

This is exactly why Game Compressor warns you when you select a game that uses DirectStorage for compression. item.title: These 6 ESP32 projects prove that plugging everything into a wall was never the right answer
item.itunes:title: These 6 ESP32 projects prove that plugging everything into a wall was never the right answer
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Every ESP32 project I’ve built followed the same path. I found an outlet, ran a cable, and plugged it in. That’s the easiest way to get something working. When I started placing sensors away from the desk, I ran short of wall outlets to power those ESP32 boards. It made me question whether every build needs to draw power all the time.

Some of the builds didn’t care whether they were wired. Others, like sensors screwed into a window frame or an exterior wall, were far more awkward with a permanent cable. Now I sort projects by power source before picking up a single part and building them using ESPHome in Home Assistant. These six are the ones where the battery is the better choice.

4 simple ESP32 projects you can build without any sensors

Not all ESP32 projects need to involve extra sensors or circuit components

By  Ayush Pande

Door and window sensors

There’s no outlet inside a window frame

A reed switch and an ESP32 make one of the simplest sensors you can build. It tells you whether a door or window is open or closed. A wired version only works if you run a cable through the frame, but the battery offers another way.

The sensor can sleep until the magnet moves, wake up on that change, report the new state to Home Assistant, and go straight back to sleep. That wake-sleep-report cycle is the pattern behind every build in this list. A single Li-Ion 18650 cell or three AA/AAA cells with a regulator can easily last a few months, depending on how often the door opens. Pick a board with a low deep-sleep power draw, since some development boards waste power on the USB chip and LED.

Water leak sensors

Leaks start where you’d the least want a mains cable

If there’s one sensor that can convince a smart home skeptic, it’s this one. The SEN18 water level sensor sits on the floor, and when its exposed end touches water or moisture, the reading changes. The ESP32 wakes up every few minutes, checks the reading, reports a leak to the Home Assistant if it crosses your set threshold, and goes back to sleep. That means a short alert delay, but it doesn’t need constant power.

Battery also suits the placement, as you can tuck it under sinks, behind washing machines, next to water heaters, and near water tanks. These areas are damp, and a battery-powered build makes more sense than a live cable on the floor.

7 sensors under $10 that completely changed my smart home

You don't need to splurge to build a smart home

29
By  Samir Makwana

Driveway motion cameras

Deep sleep until something moves

Camera-centric local-first Ring doorbell alternative build needs mains power because continuously streaming video draws far more current than a battery can sustain. That said, the driveway camera doesn’t have to work that way.

Pair a camera-equipped ESP32 with a motion sensor (a PIR sensor works well), and the build only activates when something moves in the driveway. When it detects movement, the board wakes from deep sleep, takes a snapshot, sends it to Home Assistant, and goes back to sleep again. You lose the live feed, but you gain a battery that can last weeks instead of a permanent power run to wherever the camera sits. Just check the board’s deep-sleep power draw, since some ESP32-CAM boards consume more than you’d expect.

Soil moisture sensors

They need to wake only twice a day

Building gardening sensors with a relay and water pump needs continuous power. But if you only need moisture data to know when to water your garden, that’s overkill. With an ESP32 board, you can use a capacitive soil moisture sensor to check the moisture levels twice a day, report it to Home Assistant, and then go back to sleep. Powering the sensor only during the reading cuts the drain even further.

A small battery, optionally topped up with a solar panel, can power the build for months. Running a live cable to a raised bed or patio pot was never realistic anyway, so a battery-only node makes sense.

Remote temperature nodes

The shed and attic never had an outlet

I’ve used a temperature and humidity sensor to replace branded smart home sensors before, but it lived near a plug. The same sensor works just as well in a shed, garage, or attic, none of which has an outlet. Instead of pulling a long wire, a battery does the job.

Checking every few minutes is enough for most automations, and the ESP32 can return to deep sleep in between. You can send the readings to a Home Assistant dashboard and use them to drive HVAC-centric automations. Extreme heat and cold do affect battery performance, so expect shorter runtimes in an attic or unheated shed. Also, check your Wi-Fi coverage out there, since a weak signal keeps the board awake longer and drains the battery.

BLE presence tags

It just needs to say hello occasionally

The Bluetooth proxy I built has no gimmicks and no cloud service. It just sits quietly in a corner listening for Bluetooth devices around my house. A battery-powered presence tag is the other part of the setup, and it’s small enough to clip to a bag or keychain that periodically announces itself for the proxy to pick up.

There’s no display or sensor to read, and nothing happens more than a few times a minute. That makes it one of the most power-efficient ESP32 builds, though battery life depends on how often the tag advertises itself. Plugging it into the wall would just defeat the point.

Your first ESP32 project shouldn't be a weather station — it should be a box of 30 random sensors

The ESP32 can be daunting at first, but a weather station to start off with is a rookie mistake.

7
By  Adam Conway

Choosing a power source is a conscious design decision

None of these projects require a battery, and I’m sure someone has run an extension cord to power most of them. But in every case here, the cable fights the placement, the duty cycle, or the point of the build. Designing every project around the wake-sleep-report cycle from the start made planning much easier.

Using a battery with an ESP32 isn’t automatically easier. Configuring deep sleep adds firmware complexity, especially if you want the board to report when the battery needs charging or swapping. It’s extra work, but for these six, it pays off.

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I often need to create diagrams to explain ideas, workflows, and technical concepts, but I don't always want to pay for a dedicated application to do it. Microsoft Visio is one of the obvious choices, but I wanted something simpler that could still handle serious diagramming work. I started looking at free options and came across draw.io. I had seen the name before, but never really considered using it as my main diagramming tool. This time, I decided to give it a proper try instead of assuming a free tool would come with too many limitations. What I found surprised me.

draw.io looked too simple in the beginning

It looked simpler than I expected

When I first opened draw.io, I honestly wasn't expecting much. The interface looked clean and fairly basic. There wasn't a lot happening on the screen, and I initially wondered whether I had found a proper Visio alternative or just another lightweight diagramming tool.

I decided not to judge it too quickly and spent a little time exploring the interface. That was when I started noticing that simplicity was actually one of its strengths. The layout was easy to understand, and I didn't have to dig through complicated menus just to figure out where things were. I could quickly find the canvas, toolbar, panels, and basic controls without needing a tutorial.

I also liked that draw.io didn't try to overwhelm me during the first few minutes. Everything felt straightforward, and I could start experimenting almost immediately. There was no long setup process or unnecessary account creation getting in the way.

I also use the alignment and positioning controls whenever I want things to look cleaner. They make it easier to keep elements properly spaced without manually adjusting every little detail.

I can also enable additional shape libraries when I need something specific, which gives me even more options to work with.

The templates are useful when I don't want to start from a completely blank canvas. I can pick a starting layout, replace the existing elements, and adapt it to what I'm trying to create. This saves time when I'm working on a familiar type of diagram.

These options don't feel like they're there just to make the feature list look impressive. I actually use different libraries depending on what I'm working on. I don't need a complicated setup or a paid subscription just to create diagrams for my work. draw.io fits into my workflow without making diagramming feel like another task I need to manage. It has also become one of those tools I can open whenever an idea is easier to explain visually. I started looking for a free Visio alternative, but ended up finding a diagramming tool I genuinely want to keep using.

Draw.io

item.title: The 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 get a price hike as keeping the price low becomes "unsustainable"
item.itunes:title: The 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 get a price hike as keeping the price low becomes "unsustainable"
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • The 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 get a $12.50 price hike; now $67.50 (Pi 4) and $77.50 (Pi 5).
  • Foundation blames rising RAM costs — holding prices on 2GB variants became unsustainable.
  • Consider Pi 3 models, an ESP32, or a mini PC instead of purchasing a powerful Raspberry Pi model.

The RAM crisis has not been kind to the Raspberry Pi, which has seen a few price hikes over the last year. Back in April 2026, the foundation announced that it was increasing the price of a few boards, but sparing the 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 and 5.

Now, that, too, has become too much to bear, as the foundation has announced a price increase.

The 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 get a $12.50 price hike

The cost of RAM was a driving factor

As announced on the Raspberry Pi official website, people will need to pay a little extra for a new Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 with 2GB of RAM. As the foundation explains, it has tried its best to keep the prices low, but things were getting troublesome:

During our last round of price increases, in April, we were able to hold down the price of the 1GB and 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 and Raspberry Pi 5 products, while increasing the price of higher-density variants. This has now become unsustainable, and from today we are increasing the price of the 2GB variants by $12.50, to $67.50 for Raspberry Pi 4 and $77.50 for Raspberry Pi 5.

The foundation follows up by reminding everyone that sometimes people buy an SBC that's far too powerful for their use case, and it urges potential buyers to research whether a Raspberry Pi 3B, 3A+, or 3B+ would better suit their needs. It also points to its Raspberry Pi Approved Resellers program as the best way to ensure you're not overpaying for your SBC.

Unfortunately, this is just one data point in an ongoing trend with Raspberry Pi as the foundation navigates this new world of hardware pricing. Besides the previously-mentioned April price hike, Raspberry Pi had one in December 2025 and February 2026, also due to RAM becoming more expensive.

While it is smart to reassess whether you truly need the beefier Raspberry Pi models for your projects, now may also be a good time to consider whether an ESP32 might be a better fit. We've even had success replacing them with a mini PC.

Cytron's cheaper Raspberry Pi 4 boards are a solid deal if you can live with 30% less speed

A bit of give and take.

By  Simon Batt

item.title: I ignored Home Assistant's map for years until the new beta made it worth opening
item.itunes:title: I ignored Home Assistant's map for years until the new beta made it worth opening
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If there's one thing I have never even touched in Home Assistant, it's the map. Sure, it was novel when I first launched Home Assistant and thought, "Oh, cool, I can mark where my smart home is," but that was about it. I never revisited the sidebar entry. I didn't even notice the change in provider, caused by the existing mapping platform requiring an API key. Now, Home Assistant draws the map and caches it locally using OpenStreetMap. And it turns out, this is quite the large deal.

The latest Home Assistant beta for October (2026.10) is focused on this new mapping frontier, and we've taken it for a quick spin.

The new map looks awesome

I must admit, I do enjoy using OpenStreetMap. It absolutely has nothing on Google Maps when it comes to quickly finding an activity to do or working out where to grab a bite to eat, not to mention directions for journeys, but for general browsing, OSM is perfectly servicable, and it looks great. Running it on phones and desktop PCs is easy through Home Assistant too. It's cached, so if the net drops for a sec, you can still browse downloaded vectors, and the Open Home Foundation has built some features on top of this new platform.

Thanks to the switch, we now have a much crisper view. It looks awesome. Zooming in and out, panning across landmasses, it's all butter-smooth, so long as your underlying device has the horsepower to keep up. The old mapping system is still hanging around, but it's only called upon if your device (like an old wall-mounted tablet) isn't running the new map too well. Markers have been completely redesigned and now use photos with specific colors. It's easier to see multiple people at a single location too, thanks to them grouping together.

The entire map dashboard has been given a fresh lick of paint. There's an overview, located next to the map on the desktop and as a pull-out drawer on mobile. Three tabs are present, one dedicated to people, a second to devices, and a third to zones. Selecting a person will show recent activity, as well as which zones they were present in. This same overview can be shown through the dashboard card, which can be pinned to your profile's default landing page. It's all pretty awesome.

What are these zones?

Speaking of zones, you can now set zones on the map and see if people are present there. For instance, you may have a zone for the house, another for the gym, a third for your place of work, and maybe one more for a best friend's house. So long as the installed apps have the relevant location permissions set, you should be able to keep tabs on one another and ensure the entire family is safe. We'd be the last ones to use location-based tech like this to check on one another, but it's a cool addition to play with, especially for scripts.

The new Maintenance dashboard is the Home Assistant feature I did not know I needed

This dashboard makes it easy to check the battery levels on my Home Assistant entities

1
By  Ayush Pande

Home Assistant is becoming more social

Without all the bad stuff that comes from social media platforms

Profiles didn't really do much in previous Home Assistant versions. Okay, they did, but you never really bothered with them outside of creating users, setting permissions, loading a default dashboard, and calling it a day. That's all set to change with 2026.10. Clicking the username at the bottom of the sidebar loads up the refreshed user profile. This is now an overview of your Home Assistant account, whereas before it would simply be dumped with data to parse through.

Appearance settings will allow you to alter the default dashboard and the order of menu items in the sidebar. Localization handles languages and time zones, as well as how everything is rendered (DD/MM/YYY is the correct way with a 24-hour clock, by the way). Then there's an option to alter how notifications, display, and shortcuts are handled for this particular device—it changes depending on which client is being used, be it a phone or desktop PC.

Oh, and now you don't have to handle requests from family members to have their profile photos changed. They can now do it themselves. This was such a strange requirement for Home Assistant and was just another reason why we never really bothered. Everything felt like such a hassle, which is what makes 2026.10 pretty solid so far.

Home Assistant's latest beta finally turns your Android phone into a voice satellite

You can now use your phone as a true voice assistant for Home Assistant.

By  Adam Conway

This beta continues to make improvements

Automations continue to receive development love

Home Assistant is great for creating automations, and improvements have been made over the year or so to perfect the user interface, but the team just scored another win with 2026.10. Triggers could be configured with the "triggered by" condition set to do something, depending on which triggered is ... well, triggered. You'd have to enter an ID and then remember which one it belonged to. No one used it, and it largely went unnoticed anyway.

That's all changed with this beta. Adding a "triggered by" condition brings up available triggers as part of the automation. There's even an ordered list, depending on which is displayed first. The software tackles everything in the backend, and it's one less thing for us humans to worry about, which is precisely the point of a smart home. To make all our lives that little bit easier. But this isn't everything, as integrations have been added and featured, so be sure to check the official beta blog post for more details.

The beta is available for testing right now

Ready to take the plunge? Fire up a test instance of Home Assistant OS and join the beta program via the settings area. 2026.10 beta will continue running for the next couple of days, with the full release slated for launch on Wednesday, October 7th. This update might just get me to start seriously using the map and working on more location-based automations, which could work wonders for our automated heating system for the coming winter months.

item.title: A Raspberry Pi is a better addition to your TV than a Chromecast
item.itunes:title: A Raspberry Pi is a better addition to your TV than a Chromecast
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Chromecast was revolutionary when it launched because it turned your normal TV into a system capable of running multiple streaming apps. Even a smart TV that dropped support for apps could gain a new life with a Chromecast. However, there have been several Chromecast iterations, and now the cheaper alternatives are being phased out to make room for the Google TV streamer, which starts at $100. However, you can use a Raspberry Pi as a Chromecast replacement to enjoy a better TV experience.

Raspberry Pi is capable of reviving your TV with multiple operating system options and apps. You can choose an operating system, customize it to your liking, or switch to a different one. The freedom to use local playback, add-ons, or integrate your streaming server with the Pi is a nice-to-have feature. Let's explore how a Raspberry Pi can surpass Google's streaming solution and become a worthy addition to your old TV setup.

No OS confinement

Pick whatever you like

When you buy a Chromecast, you're bound to Google's OS or a custom version of Android, along with pre-installed apps. You cannot expand storage (in some models) or switch to another operating system if you like. Chromecast doesn't give you the liberty to swap OSes or perform much customization, or install apps from anywhere except the official store.

A Raspberry Pi has the ability to run customized versions of TV OS that can comfortably run on it. It also offers a lot of variety, ranging from LineageOS, OSMC, and LibreELEC, among others, that you can choose from. You don't need to sign up or agree to a telemetry agreement just to watch TV or stream video.

As your TV ages, the UI and apps load slowly, which can ruin the overall experience. Even if your Pi becomes outdated or lacks power, you can switch to a lightweight TV OS. You can choose from different UIs and themes, all designed to make the new OS more user-friendly. Chromecast might drop support for very old models, but a dedicated community TV OS might continue longer.

Limited storage

Not as versatile as you expect

Chromecast is a streaming device with limited storage for apps. Since it only streams content, there's less focus on storage. However, as your app library grows, the limited storage space becomes a problem, forcing you to switch between apps. On the other hand, a Raspberry Pi gives you the freedom to pick the storage size and type. You can use an SD card, a USB drive, or an NVMe drive, depending on the type of support your Pi offers.

Faster storage paired with an equally capable processor can handle high-resolution streaming and direct video playback. You can even play games directly within the Kodi UI, or simply swap the SD card in the Pi for Lakka or RetroPie. It's an additional perk of connecting a Raspberry Pi to your screen, where you just need to put the games on the boot drive.

Better connectivity options

Lots of ports

  • Credit: RyzerPhenix/MakerWorld
  • Credit: TAKA@P.P.R.S (Flickr)
  • Credit: RyzerPhenix/MakerWorld
  • Credit: TAKA@P.P.R.S (Flickr)

If your TV lacks additional ports, such as Ethernet or USB, and the original ones no longer work, a Chromecast can't help you. Even with models that support connecting a USB drive, you need to use a specific file format.

A Raspberry Pi offers numerous connectivity options, enabling you to connect devices and establish a network connection. For example, you can connect an external hard disk or SSD to the Pi’s USB port whenever you want to play media from it. Therefore, you can now add I/O options that previously did not exist.

The same goes for adding Wi-Fi or Ethernet capabilities to the TV. Since the Raspberry Pi offers various wired and wireless connectivity options, streaming content over a network isn't a problem. I suggest using the Ethernet connection for reliability, but you can choose any connection mode.

Chromecast offers Ethernet connectivity in some newer models (Google TV streamers have a dedicated Ethernet port), but you need to purchase a separate adapter. It disrupts the entire connection layout, but if you opt for a Raspberry Pi, all ports, including Ethernet and faster USB 3.0, are available on the board.

You don't need to connect USB hubs or adapters to it. Only one cable is required to connect the Pi to the TV, and one power adapter is needed to power the Pi.

You’re in control

Choosing a Raspberry Pi as a streaming device is a good decision if you want to have control. But it comes with a price: setting everything up. It’s a self-hosted project, so you’ll have to take control. The next step is to pick a compatible OS for your Pi that doesn’t slow down when you try running apps on it. It’ll take some effort, but the rewards are worth it.

After installing an operating system that mimics a TV OS, you need to set up apps, attach local storage and a network share, install additional subtitle tools, and more. Your TV remote can handle most tasks, but you can use an IR remote and plug its receiver into the Pi to control it.

Kodi’s add-ons are the best part because you can add several services, such as YouTube, which plays without ads. Don’t hesitate to explore Kodi add-ons because that’s where the magic happens if you go with a Kodi-centric OS. Netflix and other popular streaming apps aren’t a good experience if you go the Raspberry Pi way, so keep that in mind as well.
